title: Baking a cake from scratch
learner_summary: Ava, a college student who has only ever baked cakes from a box mix. She wants to make a cake from scratch, and has never measured flour, chosen a leavener or judged when a cake is done on her own.

objectives.text: Measure a cake's ingredients accurately, and explain why weighing flour or spooning it into the cup works better than scooping it from the bag.
Explain what makes a cake rise, including the difference between baking soda and baking powder, and what goes wrong when it does not rise.
Tell when a cake is done, and diagnose common problems such as a sunken middle, a dry cake or a domed top.

facts.text: A cake rises because a leavener makes carbon dioxide gas in the batter, and the bubbles expand in the oven's heat until the cake's structure sets around them.

Baking soda is a base that needs an acid in the recipe, such as buttermilk, yogurt or lemon juice, to make carbon dioxide; baking powder already contains both baking soda and a dry acid, so it only needs liquid and heat.
Baking soda and baking powder cannot simply be swapped one for one: baking soda is about three to four times stronger, and without enough acid it leaves the cake flat with a soapy or metallic taste.
Oven temperature affects the rise: if the oven is too hot, the outside sets before the inside finishes rising, which gives a domed or cracked top.

Baking time depends on the size and depth of what is baked: at the same oven temperature, cupcakes are done much sooner than a full layer cake, so a recipe's time is a guide and the cake must still be checked for doneness.

misconceptions.text: Baking soda and baking powder are the same thing and can be swapped one for one.
misconceptions.correction: Baking soda needs an acid in the recipe to work and is about three to four times stronger; baking powder brings its own acid. Swapping them one for one leaves the cake flat, or bitter and soapy.

misconceptions.text: Oven temperature and baking time do not really matter, as long as the cake gets baked.
misconceptions.correction: Temperature controls how fast the outside sets compared with how fast the cake rises, and time decides whether the middle is cooked: too hot gives a domed or cracked top, and too short a time leaves a raw middle that sinks.

misconceptions.text: Salt is not important in a cake, so it can be left out.
misconceptions.correction: A small amount of salt brings out the cake's flavor and balances the sugar; without it the cake tastes flat and overly sweet.

misconceptions.text: Scooping flour straight from the bag with the measuring cup gives the right amount.
misconceptions.correction: Scooping packs the flour into the cup, so it holds noticeably more flour than the recipe means, which makes the cake dry and dense; spoon the flour in and level it, or weigh it.

misconceptions.text: Baking measurements can be eyeballed like cooking, so a little extra of an ingredient does not matter.
misconceptions.correction: Baking is chemistry: small ingredients such as leaveners work in exact amounts, and too much baking powder makes a cake rise too fast and collapse, or taste bitter.
